title: "ADCP 1.1 documentation"
---

::: {.callout-note}
The CCSB page for this version says it is under construction. For now it gives a few example
runs that show the new capabilities of version 1.1.
:::

To run these examples, download the [receptor](https://ccsb.scripps.edu/adcpv11/download/436/)
and the [ligand](https://ccsb.scripps.edu/adcpv11/download/471/) for PDB 3Q47.

## Create a target file

This command computes the target file `3Q47.trg`:

```bash
agfr -r 3Q47_recH.pdbqt -l 3Q47_pepH.pdbqt -asv 1.1 -o 3Q47
```

`agfr` runs AutoGridFR, which computes target files.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-r` | the receptor, here as a PDBQT file |
| `-l` | the ligand, here the crystallographic peptide. When a ligand is given, agfr defines the docking box as the ligand's bounding box with 4 Å padding. |
| `-asv 1.1` | compute the preferred starting ligand positions in the box with AutoSite 1.1, rather than 1.0, which is meant for small molecules |
| `-o 3Q47` | name of the target file to write (`3Q47.trg`) |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## Run ADCP with modified amino acids

```bash
adcp -T 3Q47.trg -s "n<BHD>pis&dvd" -N 2 -n 2000 -L swiss -w testDir -o testNSAAandD
```

In version 1.1 the peptide sequence can contain non-natural amino acids, written as
**`[&]x<NAME>`**:

- The optional `&` makes the amino acid D instead of the default L chirality.
- `x` is the coarse bead that represents the side chain. Any one-letter code of a natural amino
  acid can be used here.
- The modified side chain's name goes between chevrons, `<>`.

In the example, the first amino acid is represented as an asparagine in the coarse model, and an
asparagine derivative side chain (BHD) from the Swiss side-chain library is used for the
full-atom representation. The peptide also contains a D-aspartic acid at position 5.

::: {.callout-tip}
The modified side chain is loaded from a library file, here the Swiss library selected with
`-L swiss`.
:::

This example runs only 2 Monte Carlo searches (`-N 2`) of 2000 evaluations each, so that it
finishes quickly; it is not meant to find real docked poses. It writes two files into the
working directory `testDir` (`-w`):

- `testNSAAandD_out.pdb`: a multi-model PDB file with the docked poses
- `testNSAAandD_summary.dlg`: the docking log

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

## OpenMM minimization

ADCP 1.1 can minimize docked poses with OpenMM and re-rank them. These examples assume you
already know the standard ADCP options.

### Re-ranking poses of standard amino acids

The option `-nmin` turns on OpenMM minimization of poses, followed by re-ranking. This example
docks the peptide `grctksicfpd` into the receptor from `3Q47.trg` and minimizes the top 5 docked
solutions with OpenMM:

```bash
adcp -O -T 3Q47.trg -s "grctksicfpd" -cyc -N 5 -n 100000 -w testDir1 -o example1 -nmin 5
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}

Besides the default ADCP output, this command writes:

- `example1_omm_rescored_out.pdb`: the minimized and re-ranked top solutions (receptor + peptide)
- `testDir1/example1_omm_amber_parm/`: Amber topology and coordinate files for each re-ranked
  solution, for further analysis or free-energy calculations with molecular dynamics or other
  molecular mechanics methods

### Additional options

The number of minimization steps (`-nitr`), the solvent environment (`-env`) and the output order
of re-ranked solutions (`-dr`) control the minimization. For example:

```bash
adcp -O -T 3Q47.trg -s "grctksicfpd" -cyc -N 5 -n 100000 -w testDir1 -o example1 -nmin 5 -nitr 500 -env implicit -dr -reint
```

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-nitr 500` | 500 minimization steps for each docked pose |
| `-env implicit` | minimize in implicit solvent (default: vacuum) |
| `-dr` | report minimized solutions ordered by docking score, best to worst (default: OpenMM ranking score) |
| `-reint` | rank by interaction energy (E~complex~ − E~receptor~ − E~peptide~) instead of (E~complex~ − E~receptor~) |

### Minimizing poses that are already docked

- **Post-docking minimization (`-pdmin`)** applies OpenMM minimization to poses that were already
  docked. ADCP skips docking and minimizes the poses from the earlier output file. Use the same
  target file (`-T`), job name (`-o`) and sequence (`-s`) as in the docking run.
- **Resume a failed minimization (`-resumemin`)** continues an interrupted minimization and
  re-ranking. It works only together with `-pdmin` and without overwriting (`-O`).

### Non-standard amino acids

The default force-field parameters for OpenMM minimization lack most non-standard amino acids.
ADCP therefore uses the "sannerlab" OpenMM parameter set for 182 non-standard amino acids and the
"swiss" set for 20 non-terminal ones. These sets are designed for the Swiss non-standard amino
acids and need proper licensing from the developer of the SwissSideChain database. The full list
of supported residues is in `ADCP/data/openMMff/AVAILABLE_PARAMETER.dat`.

When no OpenMM parameters exist for a non-standard amino acid, ADCP uses pdbfixer (v1.8) to
replace it with a standard one. If pdbfixer cannot replace it, the residue is mutated to alanine
for the OpenMM re-ranking.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `-F` | which OpenMM parameter sets to use from `ADCP/data/openMMff` (`swiss`, `sannerlab` or `none`); `none` turns off all system default sets |
| `-f` | user-supplied OpenMM parameters for new or unlisted non-standard amino acids (see below) |

`-f` needs three files in the same directory with the same stem. For `-f ./XXXX_ff.xml` the
program expects a force-field file `./XXXX_ff.xml`, a bond definition file
`./XXXX_residues.xml` and a hydrogen definition file `./XXXX_hydrogen_def.xml`.

## Non-canonical amino acids

ADCP 1.1 docks peptides that contain non-natural amino acids (NSAAs). Each NSAA has a name (for
example PTR), and ADCP reads its side-chain parameters from library files given on the command
line (`-l` and `-L`). ADCP ships with a library for the natural amino acids (always loaded) and a
library of fluorinated amino acids.

We also developed parameters for all amino acids of
[SwissSideChain](https://www.swisssidechain.ch/index.php). Its license will be replaced by
CC-BY 4.0, and we have been granted the right to distribute the ADCP library for this set of
[209 amino acids](https://www.swisssidechain.ch/data/family_table.pdf) in D and L forms.

The library covers 182 of the 209 SwissSideChain amino acids, in both L and D chirality. This
lets ADCP handle every non-natural amino acid currently found in the Protein Data Bank. To use
peptides with NSAAs at any position in OpenMM, we:

1. **Computed partial charges.** SwissSideChain's charges were designed for NSAAs away from the
   peptide termini, so we computed charges for terminal and non-terminal forms with the R.E.D.
   server (RESP ESP charge Derive), using GAMESS, following
   [this tutorial](https://upjv.q4md-forcefieldtools.org/Tutorial/Tutorial-3.php#11). Each form
   was capped with ACE and/or NME.
2. **Found force-field parameters.** `parmchk2` from AmberTools identified the Amber parameters
   needed (bonds, angles, dihedrals, impropers, electrostatics, van der Waals) from the R.E.D.
   mol2 files, written as an frcmod file.
3. **Built FFXML files.** ParmEd converted the frcmod and mol2 files into OpenMM FFXML files for
   each variant. These were merged into one file covering all parameters for 184 NSAAs, which
   OpenMM can load.

To use these parameters in OpenMM we also changed how each structure is loaded, cleaned and
simulated:

1. Kept pdbfixer from removing or swapping NSAAs, by loading the residue definition file and
   editing `pdbfixer.nonstandardResidues`.
2. Added `OXT` to C-terminal NSAAs. pdbfixer adds hydrogens with Modeller and handles N-terminal
   residues correctly, but not terminal NSAAs.
3. Overrode the default hydrogen definitions, to add NSAA-specific ones or apply specific
   parameter sets to residues with identical names (for example ORN).
4. Gave residues with identical molecular structures (for example THR and ALO) their own residue
   templates.
5. Overrode PDB writing to handle 4-letter residue codes, with a modified PDB writer.
